sections.h2: Who records a deed in Belmont County
sections.html:
Deeds, mortgages and related papers go to the Belmont County recorder, whose office is in the St. Clairsville courthouse at 101 West Main Street. The job is keeping the county's land records accurate, indexed and open to the public, and more than 220 years of them are on hand. Staff can explain how the records are arranged. A title search is something you arrange separately.

Indexing is the part sellers rarely notice. Each document is indexed so a searcher can build a chain of title, showing every owner and every debt attached to the land. That is what lets a title company find a deed, a lien or a release years later. The files include farm deeds, home mortgages, oil and gas leases and military discharge papers.

The recorder's online calculator follows Ohio Revised Code 317.32. Belmont County does not add the optional $5 document preservation fee that the statute lets a county charge.

Belmont County Recorder fee structure
ServiceFee
First two pages of a document$34
Each additional page$8
Each indexed marginal notation (reference)$4
Document that misses the layout standard$20 extra

In the statute, the first two pages carry a $17 base fee and a second $17 for the housing trust fund. Each added page carries a $4 base and a $4 trust fund share. The trust fund share is collected under section 317.36. Other services have their own statutory rates:

  • Certified copy: a $1 base fee and a $1 trust fund fee per page, plus 50 cents and 50 cents when the recorder's seal is needed.
  • Photocopy at the counter: $1 and $1 per page.
  • Each marginal reference: $2 and $2, which matches the $4 in the table.
  • Living will or health care power of attorney: a base fee of $17 to $20 plus a matching trust fund fee.

Payment is due when the paper is handed in, except that electronic filers may settle by funds transfer or ACH afterward. Use the calculator to price a deed with several pages of legal description.

Documents must meet the standards in section 317.114, which the recorder summarizes on its document standards page. A document that falls short is still recorded, with a $20 surcharge.

  • Text set in at least 10-point type.
  • Sheets between letter size (8 1/2 by 11) and legal size (8 1/2 by 14).
  • Ink in black or blue, with highlighter left off the page.
  • Three inches of blank space above the text on page one, then an inch and a half on each page after.
  • One inch free along both sides and the bottom edge.

The rules do not apply to papers from a court or taxing authority, plats, exhibits, DD-214 discharge papers, state or federal documents, or any document signed before the law took effect in July 2009.

Section 317.08 lists what goes into the official records, which is why more than deeds pass through the counter. Items most relevant to a house sale include:

  • Deeds and other instruments that convey land outright.
  • Mortgages, with their amendments, modifications and extensions.
  • Executory installment contracts for land that run more than a year.
  • Options to purchase, which must state a specific day and year of expiration.
  • Powers of attorney and memoranda of trust.
  • Declarations and bylaws for condominiums under Chapter 5311.
  • Easements, environmental covenants and conservation easements under the listed statutes.

A recorded mortgage, option or contract stays in the public record until a release or other instrument is recorded against it. Ask a title company to check for a paid-off mortgage whose release was never recorded.

The auditor's office sits in the same courthouse and acts on the deed before the recorder does. Under section 319.202, the auditor does not endorse a deed until the grantee or a representative submits a statement declaring the value of the property, or a statement of the reason for exemption. The deed transfer desk takes calls at 740-699-2136, and the real estate desk at 740-699-2132.

A common order in Ohio counties, which the Belmont County offices can confirm, runs like this:

  1. Draft the deed with the legal description and parcel number.
  2. Take the deed and value statement to the auditor, pay the conveyance fee and get the endorsement.
  3. Present the endorsed deed to the recorder with the fee.
  4. Receive the recorded original or a return by mail.

Ask the deed transfer desk for the current conveyance rate, since counties set their own transfer tax within the statutory limit. Ask the recorder's staff whether the recorded deed can be returned by mail.

Before anything is filed, confirm that the legal description and parcel number on the new deed match the last recorded deed. Check that the seller's original signature and the notary acknowledgement are in place. Print on the right paper in the right ink, with the margins above, so the $20 surcharge does not apply. Pay the auditor first, then the recorder, and keep the receipts with your closing papers.

If you are paying off a mortgage, make sure the lender's release gets recorded after closing. The county's records will show the old loan as open until it is. Title companies usually file the release for you, but it is worth asking for confirmation. For an inherited house, bring whatever papers the title company or probate court says support the deed, since the recorder cannot repair a gap in the chain.

sections.h2: What the local market means for a seller
sections.html:
The typical owned home in Belmont County is valued at $154,900, and 73.6 percent of homes are lived in by their owners. Some 90.9 percent of residents were in the same house a year earlier, so title often sits unchanged for years and older deeds are common. The 2020 count was 31,618 housing units, 13.6 percent of them vacant. Owners spend a median $1,215 a month with a mortgage and $489 without one.

Population slipped 3.1 percent from April 2020 to July 2025. A house near Piedmont Lake, Belmont Lake or Barkcamp State Park is sold on the same recorded title as one in town.

If a deed has gaps, such as a missing heir or a lien never released, the recorder cannot fix it. Clear it up through a title company or attorney before a new deed goes on record. A cash buyer will want the same clean title a lender would, so the cleanup does not get skipped on a cash sale.

faqs.q: What is the price of recording a deed in Belmont County?
faqs.a: The first two pages run $34 and every page after costs $8. A $4 fee applies to each indexed reference, and a document that misses the layout standard costs $20 more. The county does not add the optional $5 preservation fee.

faqs.q: Where is the Belmont County Recorder's office?
faqs.a: Inside the St. Clairsville courthouse, 101 West Main Street, Ohio 43950, under the same roof as the auditor and treasurer. Deed transfers start at the auditor's desk, 740-699-2136.

faqs.q: What paper size and ink does the recorder require?
faqs.a: Letter or legal paper in black or blue ink, 10 point or larger, with no highlighter. Leave 3 inches at the top of page one, 1 1/2 inches after that, and 1 inch at the sides and bottom. Missing these standards costs $20 more.

faqs.q: Does the recorder search my title?
faqs.a: No. Staff will explain how the records are arranged but will not perform title searches. Hire a title company or attorney, and expect a lender or buyer to ask for the result before closing.

faqs.q: Do I need the auditor before I record a Belmont County deed?
faqs.a: Yes, start with the auditor. The endorsement under section 319.202 depends on a statement of value or a statement giving the reason for an exemption. Ask the recorder's staff how to deliver the endorsed deed.
